new_edges_required.source_quote: כִּי כָּל מִצְוָה הִיא קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה
new_edges_required.reason: The phrase 'כָּל מִצְוָה הִיא קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה' is a strict IS-statement identifying mitzva with complete stature/form. 'הִיא' is the Hebrew copula of essential identity — 'every mitzva IS a complete form.' This establishes that a mitzva, in its essential nature, constitutes a whole body (komah) with all its limbs including feet (raglayim). The identification is the basis for the entire teaching: because a mitzva is a complete human-like form, it has 'feet' (raglayim) through which it walks before God — and those feet can be taken by the klipa. The bechina between מִצְוָה and קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה is the structural premise of the Torah.

new_edges_required.source_quote: וְהַמִּצְווֹת נִקְרָאִים צֶדֶק, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תהילים קי״ט:קע״ב): כָּל מִצְוֹתֶיךָ צֶדֶק
new_edges_required.reason: 'נִקְרָאִים' (are called) is the canonical bechina-naming formula in Rebbe Nachman's language — equivalent to 'הוּא בְּחִינַת' or 'הֵם בְּחִינַת.' Mitzvot are named/called 'tzedek' — they share the essential nature of righteousness/justice. The proof-text (Ps. 119:172) confirms this as an established identification, not a casual metaphor. This bechina is the keystone of the Torah's re-reading of Psalms 85:14: if mitzvot = tzedek, then 'צֶדֶק לְפָנָיו יְהַלֵּךְ' (righteousness/tzedek walks before Him) means 'the mitzva walks before God.'

new_edges_required.source_quote: וַאֲזַי אֵין לְהַמִּצְוָה הַהִיא בְּחִינַת רַגְלִין, לַעֲלוֹת בָּהֶם וְלֵילֵךְ לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ-בָּרוּךְ-הוּא
new_edges_required.reason: The Rebbe says the mitzva has (or lacks) 'בְּחִינַת רַגְלִין' — a bechina of feet. The phrase 'בְּחִינַת רַגְלִין' is a direct bechina-label for the ascending dimension of the mitzva. The raglayim are not an external object but an intrinsic modal aspect (bechina) of the mitzva-as-komah-sh'lemah: since every mitzva is a complete form (edge 139-B-001), it has all limbs including feet, and those feet are the mode of ascent. The bechina 'מִצְוָה ↔ בְּחִינַת רַגְלִין' identifies the mitzva's ascending function with the concept of feet/walking.

This is the most explicit bechina marker in the Torah: 'בִּבְחִינַת' followed by the verse reference. The bracketed addition '[בִּבְחִינַת: רַגְלֶיהָ יוֹרְדוֹת מָוֶת]' identifies the klipa — specifically in its role as the entity that holds/possesses the mitzva's raglayim — with the feminine figure of Proverbs 5:5 ('the foreign woman whose feet go down to death'). In Kabbalistic tradition Proverbs 5 describes the sitra achra / 'ishah zarah' (foreign woman), the evil counterpart of the Shekhinah. The Rebbe equates the klipa's raglayim with this verse's descending feet — they are the same entity, seen from two angles: the klipa (as it functions in this Torah) and the biblical image of the 'foreign woman' whose feet lead downward to death. The structural antithesis is perfect: Package 1's raglayim 'go up before God' (raglayim la'alot); Package 2's raglayim 'go down to death' (yoredot mavet).

bechina_language_occurrences.classification: VERSE-TOPIC IDENTIFICATION — 'כִּי יִקְרָא דְּשַׁבַּתָּא הוּא' identifies the entire verse (Psalms 85:14) with the Aramaic phrase 'Yikra d'Shabata' (the honor/glory of Shabbat). This IS-statement equates the verse's subject matter with Shabbat's honor. While this is bechina-adjacent language (the 'הוּא' copula signals essential identification), it functions here as a thematic frame rather than a node-to-node bechina edge. It is captured structurally in Package 1 by the merger of שַׁבָּת / יִקְרָא דְּשַׁבַּתָּא into the mitzva-tzedek cluster. A formal edge could be proposed: יִקְרָא דְּשַׁבַּתָּא ↔ צֶדֶק לְפָנָיו יְהַלֵּךְ (= the mitzva going before God), but this would be a derived/composite node. Captured implicitly in Package 1 rather than as a standalone new edge.

concepts_examined_and_excluded.reason: The weekdays (חֹל) are the temporal setting in which the klipa operates ('כִּי בַּחֹל, שֶׁיֵּשׁ שְׁלִיטַת הַחִיצוֹנִים'). They are the background condition, not a concept equated to another by bechina. The relationship is structural/temporal: chol = when chitzonim rule. No bechina language is used to identify chol with another concept-node. Excluded as a bechina node.

Lines 6 and 9 use taanug and sha'ashuim as near-synonyms for the divine response to the ascending mitzva. The two terms are not equated to each other via explicit bechina language — they appear together as a hendiadys ('תַּעֲנוּגִים וְהַשַּׁעֲשׁוּעִים'). No bechina edge between them is formally derivable. Captured as a shared Package 3 node (taanug as dominant; sha'ashuim as variant). No separate formal bechina edge proposed.

The derech k'vushah is the outcome produced by accumulated mitzva-footsteps. The Rebbe explains 'וְיָשֵׂם לְדֶרֶךְ פְּעָמָיו' as God making a derech (a path that is a 'derech k'vushah l'rabbim'). The phrase 'הוּא נֶאֱמַר עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁהוּא כְּבוּשָׁה לְרַבִּים' (line 8) is exegetical clarification ('derech' in the verse means specifically a public, well-trodden path) rather than a bechina-identification with another concept-node. Excluded from formal bechina edges. Placed in Package 3 by shared-nature grouping with taanug.

concepts_examined_and_excluded.concept: הַהוֹלֵךְ בַּמִּדְבָּר (the one who walks in the wilderness)
concepts_examined_and_excluded.reason: Lines 7 introduces the mashal of a person walking through a pathless desert: each repeated footstep eventually creates a trodden path. This is a rhetorical analogy (mashal), not a bechina-equivalent concept. The wilderness-walker is the vehicle of the analogy; the subject (mitzva-footsteps creating a communal path for the many) is the nimshal. Excluded from bechina edges.

concepts_examined_and_excluded.concept: קָטָן שֶׁבִּקְטַנִּים (the smallest of the small)
concepts_examined_and_excluded.reason: Line 6 mentions that even a mitzva performed by the 'smallest of the small' — without proper intention and without the mitzva's full spiritual completeness — still gives God great pleasure, compared to a father's delight in his toddler's first steps. 'קָטָן שֶׁבִּקְטַנִּים' characterizes the minimum valid performer of the mitzva, but it is not equated to another concept by bechina language. Excluded.
Kavvanah is mentioned as an element that may be absent from an imperfect mitzva yet the mitzva still generates divine pleasure. It is background context, not a bechina node.

analysis_notes.note_on_brevity: Torah #139 is a focused, compact teaching (9 lines) built entirely around one structural insight: the mitzva has 'feet' (raglayim) through which it ascends before God, but during the weekdays the klipa sucks these feet, leaving the mitzva unable to ascend; Shabbat breaks the klipa's rule, allowing the mitzva's feet to rise; God takes great pleasure in the ascending mitzva; and the accumulated footsteps of many mitzvot create a worn public path. The conceptual vocabulary is small and precise: four bechina edges, three packages, twelve nodes. No cross-cutting ambiguities or complex multi-valent bechinas.
analysis_notes.cross_reference_note: The concept 'קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה' (complete form/stature) as applied to mitzvot appears in other Torahs (cf. the Kabbalistic concept of תרי"ג מצוות corresponding to the 248 limbs and 365 sinews of the spiritual body). The concept 'צֶדֶק' as a name for mitzvot is explicitly grounded in Psalms 119:172. The klipa's identification as 'רַגְלֶיהָ יוֹרְדוֹת מָוֶת' (Proverbs 5:5 = the 'foreign woman' / ishah zarah = sitra achra) is consistent with Kabbalistic identification of the sitra achra with the ishah zarah of Proverbs. Torah #277 (referenced at the end of Torah #139: 'עַיֵּן עִנְיָן זֶה לְקַמָּן סִימָן רע"ז בַּאֲרִיכוּת') develops this teaching at greater length and would provide additional bechina relationships within the same conceptual family.
